passages.t: Holy bread and Goliath's sword at Nob
passages.happening:
David comes to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech trembles when he meets him. “Why are you alone? Why is no one with you?” (verse 1).

David says that the king has sent him on a secret mission, and that he has told his young men to meet him at a certain place (verse 2). He asks for five loaves, or whatever there is (verse 3). The priest has no ordinary bread, only holy bread, and he can give it if the young men have kept themselves from women. David says they have, as always when he sets out (verses 4-5). ‘So the priest gave him the consecrated bread, since there was no bread there but the Bread of the Presence’ (verse 6).

“Now one of Saul’s servants was there that day, detained before the LORD. And his name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief shepherd for Saul” (verse 7).

David asks for a spear or a sword, since the king's business was urgent. The priest has one: the sword of Goliath the Philistine, ‘whom you killed in the Valley of Elah’, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. And David said, “There is none like it; give it to me” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
At the end of chapter 20 David left Saul's world for good. This chapter shows how low his exile begins. The anointed king arrives at a sanctuary alone, hungry and unarmed.

Nob was a town of priests near Jerusalem, within sight of the city. After the loss of Shiloh, Eli's descendants seem to have served there, where the ephod and the bread of the Presence were kept. Ahimelech was a great-grandson of Eli. Why he trembles the text does not say.

The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set out before the LORD each Sabbath. When fresh loaves replaced them, the old ones were holy food for the priests to eat in a holy place. The priest's condition reflects the law that sexual relations made a person ritually unclean until evening, and the practice of keeping soldiers ritually pure on campaign. Ahimelech bends the rule for hungry men, but he does not ignore it.

David's mission is a lie. It seems small and practical. It will cost the priests of Nob their lives.

The narrator slips a single sentence into the middle of the scene: Doeg the Edomite was there that day. He says nothing more about him until the next chapter. A reader who notices that line senses trouble. Doeg was from Edom, the land of Esau's descendants southeast of the Dead Sea, and his place in Saul's service shows the king employing foreigners.

Goliath's sword had been laid up behind the ephod as a trophy given to the LORD, as captured weapons often were in the ancient world.
passages.later:
The law gave the bread to the priests: ‘It belongs to Aaron and his sons, who are to eat it in a holy place’ (Leviticus 24:9).

Jesus told this story when his disciples were criticized for picking grain on the Sabbath. “Have you never read what David did when he and his companions were hungry and in need?” (Mark 2:25). His point was that human need, and David's mission, came before the rule about the bread, and that the law's purpose includes mercy. Matthew and Luke tell the same exchange (Matthew 12:3-4; Luke 6:3-4).
passages.hard:
In Mark 2:26 Jesus says that this happened ‘During the high priesthood of Abiathar’, but 1 Samuel names Ahimelech. Is this a contradiction?

The difficulty is real and well known. Abiathar was Ahimelech's son, the one priest who escaped Saul's massacre in the next chapter, and who later served David as priest. Matthew and Luke, telling the same story, leave the name out.

Several answers have been offered. The Greek phrase in Mark can mean in the time of Abiathar, and Abiathar was the well-known priest of David's day, who was there at Nob. Or it may name the passage by its best-known figure, the way Mark 12:26 points to the story of Moses as the passage ‘about the burning bush’. Others think it is a slip, by Mark or by an early copyist.

Readers of different convictions about Scripture weigh these answers differently. None of them changes the point Jesus was making from the story.
passages.asks: David's small lie at Nob seemed harmless. Ask what small deceptions you tell to get what you need, and who might pay for them later. And ask how you weigh a rule against a person's real need, as Ahimelech did.

passages.happening:
That day David flees from Saul and goes to Achish king of Gath (verse 10). But Achish's servants recognize him. “Is this not David, the king of the land?” They remember the women's song about Saul's thousands and David's tens of thousands (verse 11).

‘Now David took these words to heart and was very much afraid of Achish the king of Gath’ (verse 12). So he pretends to be mad. He scratches on the doors of the gate and lets his saliva run down his beard (verse 13).

“Look, you can see that the man is insane! Why have you brought him to me?” (verse 14). Achish has no need of madmen, he says, and sends him away (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Gath was one of the five chief Philistine cities, usually placed at Tell es-Safi. Achish, its king, will appear again in chapters 27 to 29, where David serves him.

There is sharp irony here. David comes to Goliath's own city carrying Goliath's sword. The servants call him the king of the land, a title he does not yet hold, and they quote the women's song word for word. His fame, which made him a hero in Israel, now puts him in danger.

David survives by acting a part. People who seemed out of their minds were often treated with fear and avoidance, and a raving man would not be counted a threat or a prize. The word for acting like a madman is spelled like the verb meaning to praise, though lexicons usually treat it as a separate word.

God's protection of his anointed does not always look dignified. The scene is about a desperate man's trick, and it gives no one leave to mock anyone who suffers in mind.
passages.later: Two psalm headings remember these days. Psalm 34 is headed ‘Of David, when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, so that the king drove him away’ (Psalm 34:1). Samuel calls the king Achish, and many take Abimelech to be a title for Philistine kings, as Pharaoh was for Egypt's; others think the heading is a later note. Psalm 56 is headed ‘A Miktam of David, when the Philistines seized him in Gath’ (Psalm 56:1).
passages.asks: David was afraid at Gath, and he got away by a humiliating trick. Ask whether you have been brought low in a way that still embarrasses you, and whether God kept you through it. And ask whether your fame or reputation has ever become a danger to you.
